stances.claim: Christmas's true reason is Jesus Christ -- the gospels' paradoxical King of all kings who stood alone in a 'kangaroo trial' before Pilate, abandoned by His closest disciples, whose throne is a wooden cross, crown a bouquet of thorns, scepter a lowly reed, and ring a rusty nail -- yet the only King who resurrected and thereby conquered sin in all eternity.
stances.rhetorical_move: paradox-as-thesis framing (humble king = the highest king)

stances.claim: Jesus is, first, a leader with a vision and a mission -- He spoke loftily, assertively, and authoritatively to His disciples (the Sermon on the Mount being the greatest teaching of all time), leaned heavily toward the poor, sorrowing, simple-hearted, and peacemakers, and opposed the hypocrite, arrogant, proud, and self-righteous.

Jesus's parables for non-disciples ended in questions -- 'Which of these three, in your opinion, was neighbor to the man who fell in with the robbers?' (Luke 10:36); 'which of them was more grateful to him' (Luke 7:42); 'what fate do you suppose the owner of the vineyard has in store for them?' (Luke 20:16) -- because they were intended 'to enable the listener to discover something for himself.'

Jesus is, second, a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction -- quoting Albert Nolan: 'a man who has the courage of His convictions... No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed.'
stances.rhetorical_move: leadership-trait two numbered framing with named-scholar citation

stances.claim: Jesus mixed with sinners, tax collectors, a Samaritan woman, a prostitute, and an adulteress -- acquiring the 'bad' reputation of being 'a glutton and a drunkard' -- but did not seek anyone's approval; He denounced sin, called for repentance, and boldly proclaimed a kingdom of God where the weak is strong, the strong is just, and the just is compassionate.

Jesus did not mince words on hypocrisy -- Matthew 23:25-27's 'Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!... You are like whitewashed tombs, beautiful to look at on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones' -- modeling the courage of conviction at full register.
stances.rhetorical_move: scriptural-illustration of trait two via prophetic-denunciation

notable_anecdotes: The Pilate-procurator-as-Spanish-governor-general comparison -- 'the rough equivalent of the governor general during the Spanish regime in the Philippines' -- translating Roman colonial administration into PH historical idiom.

The Filipino-courtroom comic insertion -- 'an alert Filipino lawyer would surely jump to his feet and would say to the judge, Objection, your honor, the answer is both argumentative and unresponsive. I move to strike it off the record. And even a half-asleep judge would probably rule, Granted. Strike it off the record.' -- the CJ-courtroom-veteran's humor inserted into devotional reading.

The throne-crown-scepter-ring iconography -- 'His throne is a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven on His wrists' -- the most concentrated single CJ image of the crucifixion-as-coronation.

Albert Nolan's 'Jesus Before Christianity' citation -- 'a man who has the courage of His convictions... No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed' -- the most extensive scholarly-religious citation in CJ's recent devotional columns.

The inverted-kingdom definition -- 'a kingdom where the weak is strong; and the strong is just; and the just is compassionate' -- three-step chiastic progression CJ uses to encapsulate the kingdom of God.
Matthew 23's whitewashed-tombs imagery -- 'beautiful to look at on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones' -- quoted at length to model Jesus's no-mincing-words posture.

one_paragraph_summary: Opening his Christmas-week reflection, Panganiban reminds readers that the reason for the season is Jesus Christ, our Lord, King, and Leader -- summarizing across two columns a sharing he delivered before a Catholic charismatic community on why Jesus is relevant today as He was two millennia ago. Jesus is hailed as King of all kings, Ruler of all rulers, Lord of all lords on earth, in the universe, in the heavens, in all of creation -- and yet the gospels present Him as a humble defendant before Pontius Pilate (a Roman procurator, the rough equivalent of a Spanish-era PH governor general), standing alone in a 'kangaroo trial,' abandoned even by His closest disciples. Asked 'Are you the King of the Jews?', Jesus answered with a question -- an answer that 'an alert Filipino lawyer would surely jump to his feet and... move to strike off the record.' Jesus is an unusual King: His throne is a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven on His wrists. His constituents betrayed Him chanting 'Crucify Him' -- yet He is the only King who resurrected from the dead and thereby conquered sin in all eternity. CJ proposes five leadership traits, with two covered in this Part 1. First, Jesus is a leader with a vision and a mission -- speaking loftily, assertively, and authoritatively to His disciples (the Sermon on the Mount being the greatest teaching of all time), leaning heavily toward the poor, the sorrowing, the simple-hearted, and the peacemakers, and opposing the hypocrite, the arrogant, the proud, and the self-righteous; teaching outsiders through parables intended 'to enable the listener to discover something for himself,' most ending in questions like the good Samaritan (Luke 10:36), the forgiven debtors (Luke 7:42), and the tenants of the vineyard (Luke 20:16). He knew He would suffer and die but also that He would be victorious. Second, Jesus is a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction -- quoting Albert Nolan's 'Jesus Before Christianity': 'a man who has the courage of His convictions... No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed.' He mixed with sinners, tax collectors, a Samaritan woman, a prostitute, and an adulteress, acquiring a 'bad' reputation of being 'a glutton and a drunkard.' He sought no one's approval, denounced sin, called for repentance, and boldly proclaimed a kingdom of God -- opposite to that preached by the Jews and Romans -- 'where the weak is strong; and the strong is just; and the just is compassionate.' His Matthew 23 denunciation -- 'Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!... You are like whitewashed tombs, beautiful to look at on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones' -- exemplifies that courage without mincing words. Next Monday: Jesus as servant leader, as leader of prayer and faith, and as leader of justice and love.
